In mathematics, a '''contraharmonic mean''' (or '''antiharmonic mean'''<ref name="Pahikkala2010" />) is a function complementary to the [[harmonic mean]].  The contraharmonic [[mean]] is a [[special case]] of the [[Lehmer mean]], <math>L_p</math>, where ''p'' = 2.

== Definition ==
The contraharmonic mean of a set of positive [[real number]]s<ref>See {{cite journal|journal=Texas College Mathematics Journal|volume=1|issue=1|date=January 1, 2005|title=Means of Complex Numbers|url=http://www.cs.southwestern.edu/txcmj/MeansOfComplexNumbers.PDF|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060909142828/http://www.cs.southwestern.edu/txcmj/MeansOfComplexNumbers.PDF|archive-date=September 9, 2006}}</ref> is defined as the [[arithmetic mean]] of the squares of the numbers divided by the arithmetic mean of the numbers:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
  \operatorname{C}\left(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n\right) &= {{1 \over n} \left(x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \cdots + x_n^2\right) \over {1 \over n}\left(x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n\right)}, \\[3pt]
                                     &= {{x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \cdots + x_n^2} \over {x_1 + x_2 + \cdots + x_n}}.
\end{align}</math>

===Two-variable formulae===
From the formulas for the arithmetic mean and harmonic mean of two variables we have:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
  \operatorname{A}(a, b) &= {{a + b} \over 2} \\
  \operatorname{H}(a, b) &= {1 \over {{1 \over 2} \cdot {\left({1 \over a} + {1 \over b}\right)}}} = {{2ab} \over {a + b}} \\
  \operatorname{C}(a, b) &= 2 \cdot A(a ,b) - H(a, b) \\
                         &= a + b - {{2ab} \over {a + b}} = {{(a + b)^2 - 2ab} \over {a + b}} \\
                         &= {{a^2 + b^2} \over {a + b}}
\end{align}</math>

Notice that for two variables the average of the harmonic and contraharmonic means is exactly equal to the arithmetic mean:
{{block indent | text = {{math|1='''A'''('''H'''(''a'', ''b''), '''C'''(''a'', ''b'')) = '''A'''(''a'', ''b'')}}}}

As ''a'' gets closer to 0 then '''H'''(''a'',&nbsp;''b'') also gets closer to&nbsp;0.  The harmonic mean is very sensitive to low values.  On the other hand,  the contraharmonic mean is sensitive to larger values, so as ''a'' approaches 0 then '''C'''(''a'',&nbsp;''b'') approaches ''b'' (so their average remains&nbsp;'''A'''(''a'',&nbsp;''b'')).

There are two other notable relationships between 2-variable means.  First, the geometric mean of the arithmetic and harmonic means is equal to the geometric mean of the two values:
<math display="block">
  \operatorname{G}(\operatorname{A}(a, b), \operatorname{H}(a, b)) = \operatorname{G}\left({{a + b} \over 2}, {{2ab} \over {a + b}}\right) =
  \sqrt{{{a + b}\over 2} \cdot {{2ab} \over {a + b}}} = \sqrt{ab} = \operatorname{G}(a, b)
</math>

The second relationship is that the geometric mean of the arithmetic and contraharmonic means is the root mean square:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
      &\operatorname{G}\left(\operatorname{A}(a, b), \operatorname{C}(a, b)\right)
  ={}  \operatorname{G}\left({{a + b} \over 2}, {{a^2 + b^2} \over {a + b}}\right) \\
  ={} &\sqrt{{{a + b} \over 2} \cdot {{a^2 + b^2} \over {a + b}}}
  ={}  \sqrt{{{a^2 + b^2} \over 2}} \\[2pt]
  ={} &\operatorname{R}(a, b)
\end{align}</math>

The contraharmonic mean of two variables can be constructed geometrically using a trapezoid.<ref>{{cite web|url= http://jwilson.coe.uga.edu/EMT668/EMAT6680.2000/Umberger/EMAT6690smu/Essay3smu/Conharm.html|title=Construction of the Contraharmonic Mean in a Trapezoid|last=Umberger|first=Shannon|publisher=[[University of Georgia]]}}</ref>

===Additional constructions===
The contraharmonic mean can be constructed on a circle similar to the way the [[Pythagorean means]] of two variables are constructed.<ref>{{cite book|title=Proofs without Words/Exercises in Visual Thinking|first=Roger B.|last=Nelsen|date=7 August 1997 |page=56|publisher=Mathematical Association of America |isbn=0-88385-700-6}}</ref> The contraharmonic mean is the remainder of the diameter on which the harmonic mean lies.<ref>{{cite book|page=217|first1=Valery A.|last1=Slaev|first2=Anna G.|last2=Chunovkina|first3=Leonid A.|last3=Mironovsky|title= Metrology and Theory of Measurement|year=2019|isbn=9783110652505|publisher=[[De Gruyter]]}}</ref>

==History==
The contraharmonic mean was discovered by the Greek mathematician [[Eudoxus of Cnidus|Eudoxus]] in the 4th century BCE.<ref>{{cite book|first=C.|last=Antoine|title=Les Moyennes|publisher=Presses Universitaires de France|location=Paris|year=1998}}</ref>

== Properties ==
The contraharmonic mean satisfies characteristic properties of a [[mean]] of some list of positive values <math display="inline">\mathbf{x}</math>:
* <math display="block">\min\left(\mathbf{x}\right) \le \operatorname{C}\left(\mathbf{x}\right) \le \max\left(\mathbf{x}\right)</math>
* <math display="block">\operatorname{C}\left(t \cdot \mathbf{x}_1, t \cdot \mathbf{x}_2,\, \dots,\, t \cdot \mathbf{x}_n\right) = t \cdot C\left(\mathbf{x}_1, \mathbf{x}_2,\, \dots,\, \mathbf{x}_n\right)\text{ for }t > 0</math>

The first property implies the ''fixed point property'', that for all ''k'' > 0,
{{block indent | text = {{math|1='''C'''(''k'', ''k'', ..., ''k'') = ''k''}}}}

It is not [[monotonic]] − increasing a value of <math>\mathbf{x}</math> can ''decrease'' the value of the contraharmonic mean. For instance {{math|1=C(1, 4) > C(2, 4)}}.

The contraharmonic mean is higher in value than the [[arithmetic mean]] and also higher than the [[root mean square]]:
<math display="block">\min(\mathbf{x}) \leq \operatorname{H}(\mathbf{x}) \leq \operatorname{G}(\mathbf{x}) \leq \operatorname{L}(\mathbf{x}) \leq \operatorname{A}(\mathbf{x}) \leq \operatorname{R}(\mathbf{x}) \leq \operatorname{C}(\mathbf{x}) \leq \max(\mathbf{x}) </math>
where '''x''' is a list of values, '''H''' is the harmonic mean, '''G''' is [[geometric mean]], '''L''' is the [[logarithmic mean]], '''A''' is the [[arithmetic mean]], '''R''' is the [[root mean square]] and '''C''' is the contraharmonic mean.  Unless all values of '''x''' are the same, the ≤ signs above can be replaced by <.

The name ''contraharmonic'' may be due to the fact that when taking the mean of only two variables, the contraharmonic mean is as high above the [[arithmetic mean]] as the arithmetic mean is above the harmonic mean (i.e., the arithmetic mean of the two variables is equal to the arithmetic mean of their harmonic and contraharmonic means).
===Relationship to arithmetic mean and variance===
The contraharmonic mean of a random variable is equal to the sum of the arithmetic mean and the [[variance]] divided by the arithmetic mean.<ref name=Kingley1989>{{cite journal|last=Kingley|first= Michael C.S.|year=1989|title=The distribution of hauled out ringed seals an interpretation of Taylor's law|journal=Oecologia|volume= 79|issue=79|pages=106–110|doi= 10.1007/BF00378246|pmid= 28312819|bibcode= 1989Oecol..79..106K}}</ref>

<math display="block">\operatorname{C}(\mathbf{x}) = \operatorname{A}(\mathbf{x}) + \frac{\operatorname{Var}(\mathbf{x})}{\operatorname{A}(\mathbf{x})}</math>

The [[Index of dispersion|ratio of the variance and the arithmetic mean]] was proposed as a test statistic by Clapham.<ref name=Clapham1936>{{cite journal|last=Clapham|first=Arthur Roy|author-link=Arthur Roy Clapham|year=1936|title=Overdispersion in grassland communities and the use of statistical methods in plant ecology|journal=The Journal of Ecology|volume=24 |issue=14|pages=232–251 |doi=10.2307/2256277 |jstor=2256277 |bibcode=1936JEcol..24..232C }}</ref>

Since the variance is always ≥0 the contraharmonic mean is always greater than or equal to the arithmetic mean.

===Other relationships===
Any integer contraharmonic mean of two different positive integers is the hypotenuse of a [[Pythagorean triple]], while any hypotenuse of a Pythagorean triple is a contraharmonic mean of two different positive integers.<ref name="Pahikkala2010">{{cite journal|last=Pahikkala|first=Jussi|year=2010|url=http://www.ems-ph.org/journals/show_pdf.php?issn=0013-6018&vol=65&iss=2&rank=3|title=On contraharmonic mean and Pythagorean triples|journal=[[Elemente der Mathematik]]|volume=65|issue=2|pages=62–67|doi=10.4171/em/141 }}</ref>

It is also related to Katz's statistic<ref name=Katz1965>{{cite conference|last=Katz|first=L.|year=1965|title=United treatment of a broad class of discrete probability distributions|conference=Proceedings of the International Symposium on Discrete Distributions|location=[[Montreal]]}}</ref>
<math display="block"> J_n = \sqrt { \frac { n } { 2 } } \frac { s^2 - m } { m } </math>
where ''m'' is the mean, ''s''<sup>2</sup> the variance and ''n'' is the sample size.

''J''<sub>n</sub> is asymptotically normally distributed with a mean of zero and variance of 1.

==Uses in statistics==
The problem of a size biased sample was discussed by Cox in 1969 on a problem of sampling fibres. The [[expected value|expectation]] of size biased sample is equal to its contraharmonic mean,<ref name=Zelen1972>{{cite conference|author-link=Marvin Zelen|last=Zelen|first=Marvin|year=1972|title=Length-biased sampling and biomedical problems|conference=Biometric Society Meeting|location=[[Dallas]], [[Texas]]}}</ref> and the contraharmonic mean is also used to estimate bias fields in ''multiplicative'' models, rather than the arithmetic mean as used in ''additive'' models.<ref>{{cite conference|title=Rough Sets for Bias Field Correction in MR Images Using Contraharmonic Mean and Quantitative Index|first1=Abhirup|last1=Banerjee|first2=Pradipta|last2=Maji|conference=IEEE Transactions on Medical Imaging|year=2013}}</ref>

The contraharmonic mean can be used to average the intensity value of neighbouring [[pixel]]s in graphing, so as to reduce noise in images and make them clearer to the eye.<ref>{{cite journal|first=Sabry|last=Mitra|title=Contraharmonic Mean Filter|journal=Kajian Ilmiah Informatika Dan Komputer
|volume=2|issue=2|date=October 2021|pages=75–79}}</ref>

The probability of a fibre being sampled is proportional to its length. Because of this the usual sample mean (arithmetic mean) is a biased estimator of the true mean. To see this consider
<math display="block">g(x) = \frac{x f(x)}{m}</math>
where ''f''(''x'') is the true population distribution, ''g''(''x'') is the length weighted distribution and ''m'' is the sample mean. Taking the usual expectation of the mean here gives the contraharmonic mean rather than the usual (arithmetic) mean of the sample.<ref name=Sudman1980>{{cite book|last=Sudman|first=Seymour|year=1980|title=Quota sampling techniques and weighting procedures to correct for frequency bias}}</ref> This problem can be overcome by taking instead the expectation of the harmonic mean (1/''x''). The expectation and variance of 1/''x'' are
<math display="block">\operatorname{E}\left[ \frac{1}{x} \right] = \frac{1}{m}</math>
and has variance
<math display="block">\operatorname{Var} \left( \frac{1}{x} \right) = \frac{m E\left[\frac{1}{x} - 1\right]}{nm^2}</math>  
where {{math|E}} is the expectation operator. Asymptotically {{math|E[1/''x'']}} is distributed normally.

The asymptotic efficiency of length biased sampling depends compared to random sampling on the underlying distribution. if ''f''(''x'') is [[log normal]] the efficiency is 1 while if the population is [[gamma distribution|gamma distributed]] with index ''b'', the efficiency is {{math|''b''/(''b'' − 1)}}. This distribution has been used in modelling consumer behaviour<ref name=Keillor2001>{{cite journal|first1=Bruce D.|last1=Keillor|first2=Michael|last2=D'Amico|first3=Veronica|last3=Horton|year=2001|title=Global Consumer Tendencies|journal=Psychology and Marketing|volume=18|issue=1|pages=1–19|doi=10.1002/1520-6793(200101)18:1<1::AID-MAR1>3.0.CO;2-U }}</ref> as well as quality sampling.

It has been used longside the [[exponential distribution]] in transport planning in the form of its inverse.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Amreen|first1=Mohammed|last2= Venkateswarlu|first2=Bandi|title=A New Way for Solving Transportation Issues Based on the Exponential Distribution and the Contraharmonic Mean|journal=Journal of Applied Mathematics and Informatics|volume=42|issue=3|pages=647–661|year=2024}}</ref>
